source.title: Instruction-tuned LLMs with World Knowledge are More Aligned to the Human Brain
source.authors: Khai Loong Aw; Syrielle Montariol; Badr AlKhamissi; †. MartinSchrimpf; †. AntoineBosselut

record.file_problem: None; the text contains the full paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures LLM-to-human brain and behavioral alignment, not representational similarity between independently trained models or any of the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on a related but different construct: how well LLM representations predict human brain activity, plus how LLM perplexity relates to human reading times. These do not measure whether model representations converge with each other. Relevant LLM-to-brain results are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version. The paper's behavioral-alignment results are not included as rows because they concern reading-time correspondence rather than representational similarity.
record.test_reason: The study only measures how well LLM layer activations predict human fMRI responses (linear predictivity, plus RSA/CKA in an appendix) and how LLM perplexity tracks human reading times. It never compares the representations of two models with each other, so no result bears on V1–V7. It does not cite either original source; 'discusses' is the closest available relation, but the paper does not engage with the convergence claim either.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that instruction-tuning generally improves LLM-to-brain alignment (about 6%) but not alignment to human reading times. Brain alignment correlates strongly with model size and world knowledge. They suggest the mechanisms that encode world knowledge also improve alignment to the brain.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses linear predictivity to evaluate LLM representations against human fMRI activity, with additional RSA and CKA checks. It does not apply the original inter-model convergence measurement or test any of the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: For LLM-to-brain alignment, results are reported across three neural datasets and, in an additional analysis, across Linear, RSA, and CKA measures. These analyses do not test metric sensitivity of inter-model convergence.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction-tuning raises average LLM-to-brain linear predictivity by 6.2% (Pereira +6.9%, Blank +8.0%, Wehbe +3.8%). Some large models show little or no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instruction-tuning modestly increases LLM-to-human-brain representational alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain alignment correlates with log model size (r = 0.95 instruction-tuned; 0.92 all models), MMLU (r = 0.81) and BBH world knowledge (r = 0.68).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-to-brain alignment grows with scale and world-knowledge capability; this is a model-to-brain analogue of V1, not a test of it.

fits_no_version.finding: Instruction-tuned Vicuna-13B (0.229) exceeds vanilla LLaMA-33B (0.227) in brain alignment.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training objective, not only size, affects model-to-brain alignment.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gemma and LLaMA-2 under Linear, CKA and RSA, instruction-tuning effects are mixed by metric (e.g., RSA falls for LLaMA-2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The direction of model-to-brain alignment changes can depend on the similarity metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Brain alignment of LLaMA-7B rises during Alpaca fine-tuning; the no-instruction ablation also rises but stays lower.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Both added data and the instruction format contribute to model-to-brain alignment gains.

record.code_released: www.github.com/brain-score/language; www.github.com/awwkl/brain language summarization; www.github.com/declare-lab/instruct-eval; www.github.com/tatsu-lab/stanford alpaca
record.problems: The brain-alignment evidence uses three English reading datasets; the authors note that Blank2014 has only 5 participants and may have greater noise. Some larger models exceed estimated noise ceilings. Several model and metric results are reported in appendices, and the epoch comparisons are shown without numerical values in the text. None of the reported measures directly addresses cross-model convergence.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's per-model brain-alignment table (Appendix G, Table 5), behavioral-alignment results (Section 5; Appendix L, Tables 9–10 and Figure 9), and further benchmark/property results were not transcribed as individual rows because they do not measure inter-model representational convergence. The study reports no results for any listed claim version.

untested.parts: No similarity between independently trained models is measured as scale or capability grows; scale is correlated only with brain predictivity.
No vision models and no image–caption pairs.
No mapping or stitching between models; the linear maps go from a model to fMRI.
No feature or circuit comparison across models.
Linear, RSA and CKA are compared only for model-to-brain alignment, not model-to-model.
No measure of how complete or plateaued model-to-model alignment is, and no causal attribution of it.

record.verdict_notes: Model-to-brain only; no model-to-model similarity is computed, so there are no verdicts. The noise ceilings (Table 6) are exceeded by some models, which complicates the scale correlations. 'discusses' is an imperfect relation: the paper neither cites the originals nor discusses convergence.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representational similarity between independently trained models as model size or capability changes.
No paired image-caption vision/language comparison or cross-modal model-to-model alignment measure.
No comparison of features or shared subspaces across training seeds.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment between models.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
Alternative similarity measures are used for LLM-to-brain alignment, not for convergence between models; no convergence-by-metric or convergence-by-input test.
No test of whether cross-model alignment plateaus or is caused by shared training data or objectives.

rows.note: The metric robustness reported is for model-to-brain alignment, not convergence between models.
rows.check: Table 8 does not fully support 'consistent'. Linear: Gemma-2B falls 0.76→0.72 and LLaMA-2-13B is unchanged at 1.08. RSA: LLaMA-2-7B falls 0.65→0.63 and LLaMA-2-13B falls 0.68→0.65. The instruction-tuning gain is mixed across metrics; the record should give per-model values. Model-to-brain only.

rows.subject: LLaMA-7B instruction and no-instruction checkpoints
rows.operation_detail: Measured brain alignment over instruction-tuning epochs and compared against an ablation trained on the same data with instructions removed.
rows.baseline: initial checkpoint; the no-instruction ablation is the comparison model
rows.value: Figure only; text states alignment rises during fine-tuning and the no-instruction model remains below the instruction model.
rows.locator: Section 4.1; Figure 1D; Appendix K, Figure 8 and text
rows.note: The text attributes improvement to both additional training data and instruction-following training; no numerical checkpoint values are stated in the text.
rows.check: The state 'partial' has no basis. The text states alignment rises over epochs and the no-instruction ablation stays lower, which is the effect as stated. Figure only (about 0.225→0.235 read from Figure 1D). Not inter-model.
